top.title: MiLaysia Fulwiley scores 14 in return as No. 9 LSU cruises past Belmont 103-45
top.description: 23 MiLaysia Fulwiley, LSU Tigers Womens Basketball take on the Belmont Bruins. November 23, 2026; Baton Rouge, LA; at the Pete Maravich Assembly Center USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect BATON ROUGE, La. (AP) — LSU senior guard MiLaysia Fulwiley returned to play Monday following a two-game absence because of an arrest and scored 14 points in the No. 9 Lady Tigers’ 103-45 victory over Belmont. Fulwiley was a starter in LSU’s first four games until her Nov. 9 arrest for allegedly attempting to flee a traffic stop. The two most serious charges — aggravated battery and aggravated assault — were dropped last Friday by Baton Rouge District Attorney Hillar Moore, and Fulwiley will enter a pre-trial diversion program to have the remaining charges of flight from an officer, resisting an officer and obedience to officers dropped. Senior guard Mikaylah Williams had eight of her team-high 20 points in the fourth quarter to help LSU (7-0) complete its season-opening, seven-game homestand. The Lady Tigers scored the first 23 points in the final quarter and led 96-35 on Lola Lampley’s free throw with 4:18 left. LSU also received double-figure scoring from Grace Knox (14), ZaKiyah Johnson (14), and Lampley (13). Fulwiley, who drew an ovation from the crowd, entered the game with 4:37 left in the first quarter and LSU in the midst of a 13-0 run to begin the game. She hit her first shot – a 3-pointer from the wing – less than a minute after entering game and followed with a layup to complete a fastbreak opportunity. Fulwiley played 17 minutes, made 6 of 13 shots and had a team-high five steals. Belmont’s first points of the game were courtesy of Chelby Jordan’s 17-foot jumper to end a 0 of 11 shooting streak. Kinley McCarn led the Bruins (1-6) with a game-high 25 points, including seven of her team’s 12 3-pointers. Up next LSU: Vs. Villanova in the Ft. Myers Tip Off on Friday. Belmont: Vs. Iowa State in the Baha Mar Hoops Championship, Nassau, Bahamas on Friday.

top.title: Did Commanders commit penalty on Daniels' spike of ball before FG?
top.description: Officials appeared to miss a penalty on Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels' spike of the ball, just before Drew Stevens' game-winning field goal in the Cincinnati Bengals ' NFL Week 11 loss at Northwest Stadium on ESPN's Monday Night Football. At least seven offensive players must line up on the line of scrimmage before the ball is snapped. As @wvcoachpence pointed out on Twitter/X , Washington "didn't have enough players on the line." A screengrab of the play shows the Commanders have six players on the line of scrimmage. "Should have been a penalty and a ten second run off," @wvcoachpence added. "Wouldn’t have been a fun way to win like that, but still would have been a win." In addition, MNF rules analyst Russell Yurk pointed out just after the game ended that the clock operator should have stopped the clock with two seconds left when Stevens' field goal hit the net. top.description: •Poor teamwork, illiquidity, others undermine efficiency – Tegbe •Power crisis requires structural overhaul – Iledare By Ediri Ejoh Nigeria’s electricity crisis is unlikely to be resolved in 2026, as the Federal Government has shifted the settlement of its N3.3 trillion debt to power generation companies to 2027, while major interventions in metering and transmission infrastructure are also expected to extend beyond this year. The Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, disclosed this during an interview with Arise News yesterday, adding that the government had paid N1.23 trillion of the debt, negotiated down from an initial N6 trillion, and was exploring options to clear the outstanding balance. These include offsetting obligations against royalties and corporate income tax, as well as engaging the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited, NNPC, to reduce gas costs for power generation companies. “We’re on track to finish paying the rest next year. Because we are looking at different ways to settle it,” Tegbe said. On the proposed debt offsets, he said: “You can’t take money with one hand and give it with the other hand. So, let’s net it off.” Tegbe attributed 80 per cent of the sector’s challenges to human and institutional factors, with technical issues accounting for the remaining 20 per cent. “I said the problem in power sector is 20 per cent technical, 80 per cent human,” he said, identifying poor teamwork, lack of coordination among operators, liquidity constraints and governance issues as major obstacles to efficiency. He also criticised past investment decisions, saying some projects were driven by political considerations rather than proper planning. “From a technical point of view, I will tell you the biggest issue: it is that we’ve been throwing money at wrong things,” he said. The minister said his ministry was reviewing ongoing projects to prioritise investments capable of improving electricity access. Tegbe recently projected that stable electricity supply could take another three to five years. He also announced plans for a $2 billion East-West Super Grid project to expand transmission capacity from about 4,000MW to 19,000MW. The proposed network would link Funtua, Gwagwalada, Ikot Ekpene, Benin, Epe and Ilorin. Procurement is under way, with completion expected within two years, according to the minister. top.description: A key component for Manchester City is available for Napoli clash Up next for Manchester City is their fifth UEFA Champions League league phase fixture tonight against Napoli at the Etihad Stadium. Enzo Maresca revealed yesterday that Manchester City had received a big boost ahead of tonight’s with a key component of City’s defence available for tonight’s clash with Napoli. Manchester City have Matheus Nunes available to play against Napoli. Matheus Nunes missed Manchester City’s 1-1 draw with Fulham due to injury. Speaking yesterday, Enzo Maresca revealed that the Portuguese international is available for tonight’s clash with Napoli. Maresca also revealed that Antoine Semenyo is unavailable for tonight’s match. Furthermore, he added that a selection of Manchester City players are battling fatigue after a heavy workload for both club and country. Maresca explained: “ Matheus is back. The only one out is still Antoine. The rest we have some doubt, in terms of tightness, amount of games. We have today’s session and then we will decide. ” “ It’s normal with the amount of games that we have. That’s why I sometimes rotate players. “ “ We need to think not about sprints but marathons – 65 games. “ “ I would like to use the strongest ones in every game. Then we would destroy them so it’s about managing them in the best way. “ How Enzo Maresca sets up his team’s defence will be worth keeping an eye on tonight. Enzo Maresca is still searching for what is the ideal balance for the Manchester City defence. Teething issues were to be expected as Maresca embeds his ideas and philosophy into his team. Throughout this season, Abdukodir Khusanov and Rico Lewis have slotted in at right-back when Matheus Nunes has been injured. Having Matheus Nunes back does shore up the right-back position for Manchester City. However Maresca constructs his defence around Nunes remains to be seen. Perhaps, it is time for Enzo Maresca to slide Josko Gvardiol across to centre-back to help with his team’s play out from the back. Playing Gvardiol alongside one of Ruben Dias, Marc Guehi or Abdukodir Khusanov should help in this regard. That would require Nico O’Reilly to slot in at left-back with Matheus Nunes at right-back but you do feel that Gvardiol at centre-back could unlock a key piece of Manchester City’s play. Matheus Nunes is back available for Manchester City when they take on Napoli tonight at the Etihad Stadium. That is welcome news for City who are an infinitely stronger team when Nunes slots in at right-back.

top.description: The University of Michigan would owe LSU $1.5 million when it flipped Bryce Underwood's commitment to the Wolverines to reimburse the SEC school for what it paid the quarterback in high school, the UM coaching staff was told. That's according to former Michigan defensive coordinator Don “Wink” Martindale, who decried the state of college football in the most recent Family Business Podcast with former NFL coach Norv Turner, his daughter, filmmaker and football insider Stephanie Turner and son, Scott. Martindale served as Michigan's defensive coordinator under head coach Sherrone Moore during the 2024 and 2025 seasons, including the fall 2024 recruiting push in which the Wolverines sought to flip Underwood's commitment from LSU. He said that Moore discussed LSU's payments to Underwood during a staff meeting. What Martindale said about Bryce Underwood "The head coach said, 'We have to pay LSU $1.5 (million) because they've been paying this kid since he was a sophomore in high school," Martindale said. Martindale did not profess to know who was going to pay the money, to whom payment would be made or whether a transaction ever took place. He also said he didn't know how much Underwood was being paid at Michigan under Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) rules, although reports have put it at $10.5 million over four years. NCAA rules prohibit colleges from offering prospective athletes payments or benefits to induce enrollment. Division I Bylaws 13.2.1 and 22.01.2 specifically prohibit recruiting inducements, including the use of name, image and likeness (NIL) compensation to influence a recruit's college choice. Martindale said he shook his head after Moore discussed the payments and questioned how a teenager receiving millions of dollars could be held accountable for his academic responsibilities. "I said, 'Look ... who's gonna make this kid go to class?'" Martindale said on the podcast. Spokespersons from Michigan and LSU, including representatives for the universities' athletic departments, didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. 'It's just not the same' Underwood, a former standout at Belleville High School and the nation's top-ranked recruit in the 2025 class, had been committed to LSU since January 2024 before changing course and choosing Michigan that November. Martindale was on staff when Underwood flipped, but departed after Moore's firing. The Wolverines reportedly put together an NIL deal worth approximately $10.5 million over four years to land the quarterback, who had emerged as one of the most coveted prospects in the country. Underwood picked the Wolverines after LSU had offered him approximately $1.5 million per year in NIL compensation, The Sporting News reported. top.description: Washington Commanders wide receiver Stefon Diggs (3) celebrates after a play during the game against the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium. Monday Night Football has a way of putting every sideline under a microscope, and the Washington Commanders’ bench got the full treatment against the Cincinnati Bengals. With Washington’s offense stuck in neutral and about four minutes left in the second quarter, ESPN’s broadcast caught Stefon Diggs shouting, “Hey, throw the [expletive] ball!” Diggs had yet to catch a pass at that point, and Darius Slay, the veteran cornerback who earned a Super Bowl ring with the Philadelphia Eagles, appeared to read the moment as a sign of trouble between Diggs and his quarterback. Darius Slay Sees Friction Between Stefon Diggs and Jayden Daniels Slay wrote Monday night: “JD and Diggs for sure got beef!” Daniels had thrown Diggs’ way only once before then, an incompletion on third-and-9 on Washington’s first possession. The Bengals led 3-0 at that point, and Washington had punted on each of its first four possessions. The last was a three-play series that gained 1 yard, coming right after Evan McPherson’s 38-yard field goal opened the scoring. Diggs entered Monday leading Washington with 386 receiving yards on 36 catches and 59 targets, and his six touchdown receptions were tied for eighth in the NFL, with a score in three of his previous four games. Daniels, meanwhile, went into halftime 8-of-11 for 85 yards. Boye Mafe had already sacked him three times, and the Commanders had managed 120 total yards while dealing with offensive miscues in the rain. That resulting field goal sealed the win, which was the first time the Commanders picked up two wins on the bounce since 2024. Interestingly, Daniels and Diggs had won Washington’s previous game together in the final minute. In that 24-21 victory over the New York Giants at MetLife Stadium on Nov. 12, Daniels hit Diggs for the go-ahead 32-yard touchdown with 57 seconds left. Diggs had six catches for 83 yards that night. Meg, take us through it … Meg’s Corner: Processing Spirit’s coach firing The NWSL Championship is complete. The Kansas City Current have their first trophy and are preparing for a celebration at CPKC Stadium featuring the Chainsmokers. (Yeah, I don’t get that last part either.) It is also the first Monday of the shortest offseason to date, and the news is newsing. The Spirit have moved on from González after not just a third championship loss but a rare final at their home stadium, Audi Field. The atmosphere in the typically rowdy Audi drained solemnly into the streets at the final whistle, marking a 2-1 KC win, Saturday. It’s worth taking a beat to sift through the reactions to this fascinating split. First, the shock. González, 44, led the team to a third-place regular-season finish, got it to the championship and finished his tenure with a 39-13-18 record across all competitions, which puts him among the top coaches from the past few seasons. Next, acceptance. The Spirit had a chance for three trophies this year between the Concacaf W Champions Cup, the NWSL Shield and the NWSL Championship. They won none of them. Add last year’s final to the mix, and change feels inevitable for a club with an owner as ambitious as Michele Kang. Ultimately, I don’t see today’s decision as a knock on González. He should be snapped up by another team, whether that’s here in the States or back in Europe. Yes, the lack of hardware played a role in the decision, but sometimes ownership makes these calls because it just thinks a coach has taken a club as far as they can and someone else needs to push the team to its ultimate goal. It worked, in a way, for Kansas City this year. We all walked out of Audi on Saturday night knowing that the Spirit would make changes after that loss. The first one has hit. top.title: Giant Study Finds Ice Baths Can Relieve Sore Muscles – But There's a Hidden Cost
top.description: (Marc Serota Collection/iStockphoto/Getty Images) Cold water can do some amazing things to the human body , and the fitness world has taken notice. Ice baths – also known as cold water immersion – have been a popular fitness and wellness trend in recent years, with many athletes and enthusiasts embracing cold plunging, in the belief that it can accelerate muscle recovery and boost athletic performance. But do ice baths really work? A giant new review in Sports Medicine – Open might well be the most comprehensive assessment of cold water immersion to date, and it suggests cold plunging does have health benefits for athletes – but those benefits come with some caveats too. "Cold-water immersion is not a one-size-fits-all recovery tool," says lead author and exercise researcher Erfan Berjisian from Edith Cowan University (ECU) in Australia. "Its benefits depend heavily on the athlete's goals, the type of exercise completed, and when the next performance session is scheduled." Ice baths have been used by athletes for decades, but are they effective? (Ivan Rodriguez Alba/Getty Images Signature/Canva) In the study, Berjisian and fellow researchers undertook an umbrella review of scientific literature on ice baths, examining 15 published reviews and meta-analyses, which covered 161 individual studies and 3,210 participants. While that huge body of research measured lots of different things in lots of different ways – and not all of the studies were of necessarily equal quality – in broad terms, the evidence consistently suggests that post-exercise cold water immersion reduces muscle soreness. Ice baths can provide relief from soreness after exercise for up to four days, the findings suggest, with the greatest benefits after high-intensity exercise. But the benefits go beyond how your muscles feel. The researchers also found that cold-water immersion reduces levels of creatine kinase in the bloodstream, which is a marker of muscle damage, with the effects evident from about 24 hours to 72 hours. Ice baths also appear to help the nervous system return to its resting state more quickly after exercise, with cold-water immersion producing improvements in heart-rate variability, although the researchers found no consistent reductions in two key markers of inflammation. As for actual athletic performance, the benefits are more complicated, and depend largely on timing. Cold-water immersion appears to temporarily improve endurance performance, but only if athletes do exercise straight away – within the first hour after immersion – with the benefits generally disappearing after that. For some athletes, that tight timeframe might be advantageous though. The Minister of Power, Joseph Tegbe, disclosed this during an interview with Arise News yesterday, adding that the government had paid N1.23 trillion of the debt, negotiated down from an initial N6 trillion, and was exploring options to clear the outstanding balance. These include offsetting obligations against royalties and corporate income tax, as well as engaging the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited, NNPC, to reduce gas costs for power generation companies. “We’re on track to finish paying the rest next year. He also criticised past investment decisions, saying some projects were driven by political considerations rather than proper planning. “From a technical point of view, I will tell you the biggest issue: it is that we’ve been throwing money at wrong things,” he said. nigeria.title: Delta attack: Nobody will kill at rallies if law catches up with them — Falana
nigeria.description: Senior Advocate of Nigeria and human rights activist Femi Falana has warned that recurring pre-election violence and political killings will persist unless perpetrators face swift prosecution and legal accountability ahead of the 2027 polls. Speaking on Channels Television ’s Politics Today on Monday, Falana described recent election-related fatalities — including killings reported in Delta State — as tragic and preventable, blaming entrenched impunity across past tragedies and political clashes. He noted that attacks on political figures and convoys are often met with little or no consequence, creating a climate where violent tactics are normalized. “The stakes are high for the political class, but in this unfortunate incident, nothing may come of it. Yesterday, we lost scores of people in Bayelsa State in what was a boat accident. What would happen? Donations have already started; who is the owner of the boat? “Nobody would have thought they were going to kill people in a rally if they know that the law will catch up with them,” Falana said. Falana urged the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA), civil society, and other stakeholders to step up rather than leaving political affairs solely to politicians. “Arrests may be made in Delta State, but I am challenging the Nigerian Bar Association and the human rights community to intervene very decisively because if we leave the affairs of our country in the hands of politicians, we will run into a serious crisis,” he said. He further called on the NBA to mobilize lawyers to help the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) prosecute electoral offenders, arguing that INEC is already stretched by pre-election and post-election litigation and lacks the bandwidth to handle prosecutions alone. Beyond electoral violence and credibility concerns — such as voter register cleanup, official accountability, and result transmission — Falana pressed political parties and candidates to campaign on concrete governance issues rather than ethnicity or religion. He pointed to unspent basic education funds at the state level, compulsory health insurance and child rights laws, fuel subsidy controversies, crude-for-loans commitments, and stalled refinery rehabilitations as areas requiring public debate and enforcement. Despite mounting frustrations, Falana rejected the idea that Nigeria is beyond hope, arguing that existing laws can drive change if citizens, the media, and civil society enforce accountability. “So for me it’s not a hopeless situation. nigeria.title: 970m Africans lack access to clean cooking — Energy expert
nigeria.description: By Ediri Ejoh & Henry Obetta About 970 million Africans lack access to clean cooking, while over 560 million people in sub-Saharan Africa are without electricity, energy experts have said, calling for greater continental collaboration to tackle the crisis. Regional Chair for Africa of the World Energy Council, Mr Omar Farouk, disclosed this at the 14th anniversary lecture and investiture into the Realnews Hall of Fame, organised by Realnews Magazine, with the theme: “Geopolitical Turbulence and Energy Security: Forging Strategic Opportunities for Africa.” Citing the 2026 Tracking SDG 7 Report, based on 2024 data, Farouk lamented Africa’s energy poverty despite its abundant oil, gas and renewable resources. “How can a continent so richly endowed with energy resources remain so energy poor? Why do petroleum-producing countries sometimes struggle to supply affordable fuels to their own citizens? Why do countries with natural gas resources suffer from electricity shortages?” he asked. He attributed the crisis largely to inadequate finance, technology and infrastructure, rather than resource scarcity. “We cannot, as a continent, be able to get out of where we have found ourselves today if we continue to operate in silos. Our solution lies in cooperation and collaboration,” he said. Farouk stressed that finance, technology and infrastructure must work together to drive energy development, adding: “You can have a lot of money without the technology, you can’t make any progress. You can bring scientists, technologists, without the money, they can’t make progress. And you can have both of these without the energy infrastructure, you can’t move energy from one point to the other.” He said Africa was projected to attract only $110 billion, or 3.3 per cent of the estimated $3.4 trillion global energy investment in 2026, while universal clean cooking access would require about $4 billion annually. Managing Director of Frazimex Engineering Limited, a subsidiary of Oilserv Group, Engr. Chuka Eze, urged African countries to leverage global geopolitical disruptions to strengthen energy sovereignty and industrial capacity. He said Africa captures less than one per cent of the value generated from clean-energy technology manufacturing, despite its rich mineral resources. “Africa’s opportunity is to move from being a supplier of strategic resources to becoming a shaper of the global energy system,” Eze said. He called for stronger local-content policies, technology transfer, skills development and regional cooperation to promote domestic processing, manufacturing and industrial growth. nigeria.title: Ajaokuta: NES blames collapse of long-term planning for 40-year stalemate
nigeria.description: By Emma Ujah, Abuja Bureau Chief The President, Nigerian Economic Society (NES), Dr. Baba Musa, has blamed the collapse of long-term economic planning for the failure of the Ajaokuta Steel Company to become operational more than four decades after its establishment. Musa, who spoke at the National Growth & Development Forum (NGDF) 2026 in Abuja, said Nigeria lost the link between economic planning and execution, resulting in the abandonment or underperformance of strategic national projects. “History demands candour. Somewhere along the way, we lost vital links between plan and performance. We built, but did not always maintain,” he said. According to him, the oil windfall of the 1970s diverted the country from agriculture and non-oil exports which had previously sustained the economy. “The oil windfall of the 1970s drew us away from the agriculture and non-oil exports that had sustained us. Strategic projects such as the Ajaokuta Steel Complex, begun with great promise, have yet to fulfil it four decades on. “And when formal planning gave way in the mid-1980s, long-term strategy too often yielded to visions that changed with administrations,” Musa said. He said Nigeria must learn from its past policy failures to avoid repeating mistakes that have undermined economic development. “The Nigeria we want must be built upon the Nigeria we have, and the Nigeria we have,” he added. The NES president also expressed concern that economic reforms had yet to translate into shared prosperity, noting that about 63 per cent of Nigerians, estimated at 140 million people, lived below the poverty line in 2025, according to the World Bank. “Macroeconomic stability is necessary, but it is not yet shared prosperity. A stable exchange rate is not yet a full dinner table. Stability is the foundation; it is not the building,” he said. Musa called for an economy that generates jobs, supports the poor, boosts domestic production, invests in human capital and promotes disciplined public finance and credible institutions. Similarly, President, Capital Market Academics of Nigeria, Prof. Uche Uwaleke, said economic reforms must be measured by their impact on citizens’ welfare, job creation, purchasing power and poverty reduction. nigeria.description: Former Deputy Senate President Ovie Omo-Agege has alleged that the gunmen who attacked his campaign team in Delta State, killing four people, repeatedly shouted his name and declared their intention to kill him. Omo-Agege, who is seeking election to the Delta Central Senatorial District on the platform of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) in the 2027 general elections, said he escaped the attack through the intervention of his Department of State Services (DSS) escorts. Omo-Agege described the incident as a premeditated attack, alleging that there had been a build-up to the violence. He questioned why he would be singled out for elimination when several other politicians were also contesting elective positions. The former lawmaker said the attackers struck less than five minutes after he began addressing supporters at the campaign venue. According to him, he had moved towards the side of his vehicle to make eye contact with members of the audience when the gunshots rang out. “It was by divine intervention. business.description: Bitcoin Magazine Strive (ASST) Buys No Bitcoin Last Week, Holdings Stay at 43,404 BTC Strive (Nasdaq: ASST) bought no bitcoin last week and sold no stock to fund new purchases, leaving its holdings unchanged at 43,404 BTC, according to a Monday 8-K filing. The Dallas-based company reported that its bitcoin count was unchanged between Nov. 13 and Nov. 20. It sold no Class A common shares, no SATA preferred shares and no SATS preferred shares in its at-the-market programs from the Nov. 13 close through the Nov. 20 close. Strive pauses after two small buys The pause follows a slowdown from the October sprint that built the stack. Strive bought 251 bitcoin for $17.5 million the prior week at an average of $69,853 per coin, after adding just 29 coins the week before that. Bitcoin traded near $61,000 on Coinbase on Monday afternoon. That is about 12.6% below the $69,853 average Strive paid for its most recent purchase. At that price, the 43,404-coin stack is worth roughly $2.65 billion. The filing gives no reason for the pause, and the company has not said whether it plans to resume weekly buying. Strive has typically disclosed its holdings on Mondays, so next week’s update will show whether the stack grows again. Most of the stack was built quickly. Strive held 28,000 bitcoin on Sept. 30 and acquired 15,124 more between Oct. 1 and Oct. 30, including a single 6,182-coin purchase. The company closed a registered offering of 7 million SATS shares on Oct. 20 for about $609 million in net proceeds, which funded much of that run. Cash and preferred holdings Strive’s cash and cash equivalents slipped to $462.4 million as of Nov. 20 from $465.3 million a week earlier, a decline of $2.9 million. The filing does not break out what drove the change. The company also still holds 505,000 shares of Strategy’s variable-rate STRC preferred stock. The fair value of that position fell to $47.3 million from $50.5 million, a drop of about $3.2 million, with the share count unchanged. Share counts were also flat. Outstanding preferred stood at 14,030,176 shares of SATA and 7,141,037 shares of SATS, the 15% perpetual preferred it has used to fund most of its purchases. business.description: Bitcoin Magazine Bitcoin Price Fades Near $61,000 as Stocks Soar on Huang’s Return The bitcoin price slipped back to near $61,100 on Monday afternoon, giving up nearly all of its morning spike even as Wall Street held one of its biggest rallies in years on Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. Bitcoin jumped above $64,000 shortly after the Nvidia news broke before 10 a.m. ET and topped out near $64,500. The move reversed within hours , and the bitcoin price dipped to around $60,800 by 2:45 p.m. ET. It remains up only modestly on the day. The round trip was costly for leveraged traders. Bitcoin liquidations reached about $321 million , with short bets making up $224 million of that total. Liquidations across the broader crypto market topped $762 million. The Nasdaq Composite was up about 6.9% near 24,170 at about 3:40 p.m. ET, while the S&P 500 gained about 5% and the Dow rose about 3.2%. The S&P 500 had fallen seven straight days before Monday. Nvidia (NVDA) led the move, trading near $165.66, up about 32% from Friday’s close of $125.53. The board voted unanimously to bring Huang back as president, CEO and director, 12 days after he resigned. A stronger dollar may be weighing on the bitcoin price. The dollar index rose about 0.65% to 104.40 , its strongest level since April 2025, as the stock rebound put more Federal Reserve rate hikes back in play. The Fed meets Dec. 8-9, and a quarter-point hike remains the base case. entertainment.title: How Mary Akinwola Graduated with a Distinction from Oxford After Receiving Multiple Scholarships
entertainment.description: Mary Akinwola graduated from the University of Oxford after receiving the Chevening and Mastercard Foundation Scholarships. My name is Mary Akinwola. I’m a physiotherapist, a strategy consultant, a healthcare entrepreneur, and I recently graduated from the University of Oxford with a distinction in Health Service Improvement and Evaluation. I have probably said that last part a hundred times since getting my results, and honestly, I don’t think I’m tired of saying it yet. Haha! One thing about me is that I like to be involved. I am sometimes curious about things that have absolutely nothing to do with what I’m supposed to be doing, and I genuinely enjoy working with people. I like organising things, bringing people together, and seeing an idea move forward to get accomplished. So I have known that going to Oxford was never going to be just about getting a master’s degree. Let me explain how I ended up there. I studied Physiotherapy at the University of Ibadan, where I graduated with First-Class Honours. During my undergraduate years, I was involved in quite a lot outside academics: student leadership, journalism, research, community health programmes and advocacy. My involvement in community health exposed me to how differently people experience healthcare depending on where they live, what they can afford and what information they have access to. I loved being a physiotherapist, and that allowed me to interrogate questions that went beyond individual patient care. Why do some people receive good healthcare while others struggle to access even basic services? How do we make healthcare more affordable? What role can technology play? It does not, by itself, explain how that light is arranged, divided or controlled. Those implementation choices can have a major influence on contrast, black level performance, highlight control and the visibility of blooming in difficult scenes. From Presence To Performance That distinction matters because a category becomes more useful to consumers when it can be evaluated through clear performance principles rather than through a technology name alone. For Mini LED, three factors provide a practical starting point. The first is hardware local dimming. In a hardware based system, physical groups of LEDs can be brightened, dimmed or switched off independently across different areas of the screen. This gives the television more direct control over how light is distributed within a single image. The second is local dimming zone count and precision. A higher number of independently controlled zones can allow the backlight to respond in smaller areas, which can improve separation between bright highlights and surrounding dark regions when other major conditions are comparable. The number itself is not the whole story, but it is a useful indicator of how granular the backlight system can be. The third is backlight architecture. Full Array Local Dimming places controllable zones across the area behind the panel, providing the physical foundation for more localized light management than designs that illuminate the panel from the edges or operate the backlight more uniformly. Together, these three elements move the Mini LED conversation from a simple question of whether the technology is present to a more useful question: how effectively is the light being controlled? He was so convinced that I wondered whether a manual somewhere explained how men were manufactured. According to him, men were created to be strong, endure pain and keep their emotions to themselves. That was simply how they were made. “So, because you’re a man, you’re not supposed to feel hurt, fear or disappointment?” I disagreed. He insisted that showing emotions was not in a man’s nature. Who made that rule? Who decided that men could experience pain but must never be seen expressing it? At what point did being a man become synonymous with pretending that everything was fine? The conversation wilted, but it has stayed with me, perhaps because my friend wasn’t expressing an unusual opinion. He was repeating a stereotype many of us have heard all our lives: “Boys don’t cry.” “Be a man.” “Man up.” Three little expressions, and somewhere between being told to be strong and learning to say “I’m fine,” I wonder how many men have forgotten what it feels like to be heard. Work nko?” “When are you getting married?” “Have you bought land?” “How is the family?” And the famous Nigerian question that can make an unemployed graduate dread family gatherings: “So, what are you doing now?” We often inquire about their achievements, responsibilities, and plans. These aspects are important, but how often do we ask about their fears? A father who leaves home before sunrise and returns exhausted, burdened by the weight of school fees, rent, and family expectations. A young graduate who has submitted countless job applications, yet still smiles politely when another relative inquires why he hasn’t found a job. A successful professional whose LinkedIn profile showcases numerous achievements, while his personal life tells a story that no one has thought to ask about. We admire their strength, we applaud their sacrifices, and we celebrate their accomplishments. But what about what they are going through? The person everyone leans on also needs somewhere to lean. sports.title: Did LSU pay Bryce Underwood in high school? Martindale was told yes
sports.description: The University of Michigan would owe LSU $1.5 million when it flipped Bryce Underwood's commitment to the Wolverines to reimburse the SEC school for what it paid the quarterback in high school, the UM coaching staff was told. That's according to former Michigan defensive coordinator Don “Wink” Martindale, who decried the state of college football in the most recent Family Business Podcast with former NFL coach Norv Turner, his daughter, filmmaker and football insider Stephanie Turner and son, Scott. Martindale served as Michigan's defensive coordinator under head coach Sherrone Moore during the 2024 and 2025 seasons, including the fall 2024 recruiting push in which the Wolverines sought to flip Underwood's commitment from LSU. He said that Moore discussed LSU's payments to Underwood during a staff meeting. What Martindale said about Bryce Underwood "The head coach said, 'We have to pay LSU $1.5 (million) because they've been paying this kid since he was a sophomore in high school," Martindale said. Martindale did not profess to know who was going to pay the money, to whom payment would be made or whether a transaction ever took place. He also said he didn't know how much Underwood was being paid at Michigan under Name, Image and Likeness (NIL) rules, although reports have put it at $10.5 million over four years. NCAA rules prohibit colleges from offering prospective athletes payments or benefits to induce enrollment. Division I Bylaws 13.2.1 and 22.01.2 specifically prohibit recruiting inducements, including the use of name, image and likeness (NIL) compensation to influence a recruit's college choice. Martindale said he shook his head after Moore discussed the payments and questioned how a teenager receiving millions of dollars could be held accountable for his academic responsibilities. "I said, 'Look ... who's gonna make this kid go to class?'" Martindale said on the podcast. Spokespersons from Michigan and LSU, including representatives for the universities' athletic departments, didn't immediately respond to requests for comment. sports.title: Giant Study Finds Ice Baths Can Relieve Sore Muscles – But There's a Hidden Cost
sports.description: (Marc Serota Collection/iStockphoto/Getty Images) Cold water can do some amazing things to the human body , and the fitness world has taken notice. Ice baths – also known as cold water immersion – have been a popular fitness and wellness trend in recent years, with many athletes and enthusiasts embracing cold plunging, in the belief that it can accelerate muscle recovery and boost athletic performance. But do ice baths really work? A giant new review in Sports Medicine – Open might well be the most comprehensive assessment of cold water immersion to date, and it suggests cold plunging does have health benefits for athletes – but those benefits come with some caveats too. "Cold-water immersion is not a one-size-fits-all recovery tool," says lead author and exercise researcher Erfan Berjisian from Edith Cowan University (ECU) in Australia. "Its benefits depend heavily on the athlete's goals, the type of exercise completed, and when the next performance session is scheduled." Ice baths have been used by athletes for decades, but are they effective? (Ivan Rodriguez Alba/Getty Images Signature/Canva) In the study, Berjisian and fellow researchers undertook an umbrella review of scientific literature on ice baths, examining 15 published reviews and meta-analyses, which covered 161 individual studies and 3,210 participants. While that huge body of research measured lots of different things in lots of different ways – and not all of the studies were of necessarily equal quality – in broad terms, the evidence consistently suggests that post-exercise cold water immersion reduces muscle soreness. Ice baths can provide relief from soreness after exercise for up to four days, the findings suggest, with the greatest benefits after high-intensity exercise. But the benefits go beyond how your muscles feel. The researchers also found that cold-water immersion reduces levels of creatine kinase in the bloodstream, which is a marker of muscle damage, with the effects evident from about 24 hours to 72 hours. Ice baths also appear to help the nervous system return to its resting state more quickly after exercise, with cold-water immersion producing improvements in heart-rate variability, although the researchers found no consistent reductions in two key markers of inflammation. As for actual athletic performance, the benefits are more complicated, and depend largely on timing. Cold-water immersion appears to temporarily improve endurance performance, but only if athletes do exercise straight away – within the first hour after immersion – with the benefits generally disappearing after that. For some athletes, that tight timeframe might be advantageous though. sports.title: Cricket's saliva ban to stay despite Gill call to overturn rule
sports.description: Bangladesh's Shoriful Islam delivers a ball on day one of the second Test in South Africa (PHILL MAGAKOE) The International Cricket Council has no plans to reverse the ban on applying saliva to shine the ball, despite India skipper Shubman Gill's call to allow the practice again. Gill on Monday said the ban should be revoked to help bowlers get reverse swing, after India's high-scoring opening Test in Wellington against New Zealand ended in a draw. However, AFP understands that the ICC has no immediate plans to relax the rule, which is treated in the same way as any other unfair method of changing the ball's condition. Saliva can materially alter the ball when mixed with sweets, chewing gum and mints and the practice is incredibly hard to monitor and regulate. The ICC temporarily barred the practice of applying saliva as a precautionary measure during the pandemic in 2020 and two years later made it permanent. The use of saliva to shine one side of the old ball and keep the other rough helps fast bowlers get the leather ball to swing late. "I don't understand why we haven't been allowed to shine the ball yet -- we are way past Covid times," Gill said after the draw. "There was a rule that you can't put saliva on the ball to make it shine. It's been seven-eight years and I still don't understand why they are not allowing it. "I think this is also a big factor (in bowlers struggling to get wickets)." The tourists had declared their first innings on a mammoth 720-9 midway through the fourth day, but New Zealand survived 120 overs to finish on 239-5 at the close. The Indian Premier League lifted its saliva ban last year, much to the bowlers' delight, but the ICC finds no reason to relax it in international matches. India and New Zealand now head to Christchurch for the second and deciding Test starting Friday, where both captains expect a more typical green, grassy and seamer-friendly wicket. fk/pst

sports.description: Washington Commanders kicker Drew Stevens is hoisted aloft by team-mates after his dramatic late field goal clinched victory over Cincinnati (Patrick Smith) The Washington Commanders scored a dramatic 22-20 win against the in-form Cincinnati Bengals on Monday, snatching victory with a Drew Stevens field goal with the last kick of the game. The Bengals looked to be edging towards victory after kicker Evan McPherson nailed a 56-yard field goal with 46 seconds remaining to put Cincinnati 20-19 ahead at the Commanders' Northwest Stadium. But Washington quarterback Jayden Daniels orchestrated a lightning-fast drive from the restart -- which included back-to-back long-range passes to receiver Antonio Williams -- to march the Commanders into field goal range as the clock ran down. Stevens then stepped up to drill a 26-yard field goal to settle an enthralling encounter that sees the Commanders improve to 4-5-1. The Bengals, regarded by many as potential Super Bowl contenders, fell to 7-3. Daniels said he had never doubted his ability to find receiver Williams for the passes of 22 yards and 42 yards that set the Commanders up for the win. "We talk about it in our offensive meeting room, it's all about trust," Daniels said. "I trusted (Antonio) to make a play for us back-to-back and he did." The wild ending was in stark contrast to the Commanders' early offensive struggles, which saw them make just 27 yards on their first four possessions. The Bengals took a 10-0 lead in the second quarter after a Tee Higgins touchdown and a McPherson field goal, before Washington's Jacory Croskey-Merritt rushed for a score to make it 10-7 at half-time. technology.title: Cisco and OpenAI pitch eBPF kernel plugins as the way to tame the patchpocalypse
technology.description: Cisco and OpenAI have released an open-source tool called Shirudo to implement compensating controls in Linux, potentially improving security for users who can’t quickly patch newly discovered software flaws. Shirudo relies on eBPF, the technology that makes it possible to run sandboxed programs in the Linux kernel. eBPF programs are effectively kernel plug-ins but don’t get unrestricted access to system resources. Developers have mostly used eBPF to create network functions that enable things like the open source Kubernetes observability and security tool Cilium , a Cloud Native Computing Foundation project. Cisco and OpenAI think eBPF can help organizations cope with the flood of 100,000-plus software flaws reported this year, many after the debut of AI-powered bug finders. The increased volume of flaws, and patches to fix them, is a problem for many organizations which already struggle to test fixes or find change windows in which to implement them. That problem has seen greater interest in “compensating controls” – changes to applications or infrastructure that harden them against flaws or malware, without requiring a patch. With Shirudo, Cisco and OpenAI are suggesting two things: The privileges eBPF programs enjoy make them a fine way to implement compensating controls for Linux; Agents should scan your infrastructure for vulnerabilities, then use tools like OpenAI’s Codex to write compensating controls as eBPF programs at machine speed. “Shirudo” is apparently the Japanese word for “shield,” so Cisco and OpenAI have called the eBPF programs the tool creates “shields.” The two companies envision humans checking every shield Shirudo creates before putting it into production. Shirudo is open source and available here . The two companies say they’ve already demonstrated it could mitigate the recently discovered flaws in Java without requiring downtime for an Elasticsearch implementation. Cisco and OpenAI are not alone in advocating for compensating controls. Third-party software maintenance outfits like Rimini Street have used them for years to protect software when their clients no longer have the right to access patches. VMware has introduced “virtual patching.” Palo Alto Networks and Rapid 7 also like this approach, and offer automation to develop controls. Where Cisco and OpenAI differ is their decision to make Shirudo open source , and their ambition that other players adapt and advance it. That offer is not entirely altruistic, as if Shirudo takes off it could create more demand for Codex. Cisco’s angle comes from the fact it owns Isovalent, an early champion of eBPF and the creator of both Cilium and the Tetragon sub-project on which Shirudo is based. Switchzilla is using eBPF in other products, so normalizing its use through an open source project can’t hurt. ®

technology.description: The leaders of the great model houses, Anthropic's Dario Amodei and OpenAI's Sam Altman, desperately want the world to believe AI is the skeleton key which will unlock the secrets of the universe. But if the AI can’t explain what it’s “proven,” are we actually any closer to understanding anything, or have we simply built another black box? That question is top of mind among mathematicians and computer scientists this week after Anthropic researcher Levent Alpöge claimed to have solved a mathematical conjecture so elusive it's gone unproven for more than 150 years. The fact that this note came out one day after Anthropic's record-setting IPO is a coincidence, we're sure. In a four-page post to his website, the researcher described how with the help of Claude, he believes he has proven the Riemann Hypothesis, one of seven Millennium problems so complex and so important that the Clay Mathematics Institute has offered a $1 million prize to anyone who is successful in solving them. The Riemann Hypothesis, conjectured by German mathematician Bernhard Riemann in 1859, contends that all nontrivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function – those with a real part between zero and one – have a real part equal to 1/2. Confused? Don’t worry. We’ve linked to an explainer that goes into more detail here . What's important is that, if the Riemann Hypothesis is right, mathematicians can place tighter bounds on the difference between the actual distribution of prime numbers and mathematical estimates of that distribution. Researchers have previously attempted to disprove the conjecture through computational brute force, and therein have shown the hypothesis holds to at least 10 trillion zeros . There’s reason to believe that the Riemann Hypothesis is accurate, but the possibility remains that over a sufficiently long series the pattern might diverge. And so, more than 150 years after Riemann published his hypothesis, it has remained just that. Alpöge’s proof, if it can even be called that, is now the subject of great debate. The four pages in which Alpöge remarks on the discoveries he and Claude made aren’t exactly a proof, but rather 14 tarballs worth of Lean code totaling roughly 240 MB. Lean is an open source programming language commonly used to help validate mathematical proofs. The Clay Mathematics Institute, which oversees the seven Millennium Problems, has promoted the Riemann Hypothesis from “unsolved” to “active” status, but it is not yet considered solved. technology.description: Don't mind the recent arrests. The ShinyHunters extortion gang may still be operating, just under the new name of Inception, according to Okta's threat intelligence group. ShinyHunters is the brash cybercriminal group that, most recently, breached rival gang Clop before hacking the FBI , resulting in at least three arrests of key suspects in September and October. The crims - and their old data leak site - have since gone dark. “While this threat cluster has changed their brand affiliation, the operators remain active in targeting organizations with voice phishing attacks and account takeovers resulting in data theft and extortion,” Okta threat hunters Moussa Diallo and Katie Nickels said on Monday. Okta tracks this threat cluster as O-UNC-053 - the “O-UNC” prefix stands for an Okta Uncategorized cluster, and it uses this label before formally attributing the activity to a named threat group. While Okta hasn't formally confirmed O-UNC-053 to be the same crime crew as ShinyHunters, the identity and access management provider’s researchers note that it does use nearly identical social engineering tactics: voice phishing , during which the scammers trick targets into entering credentials into phishing pages and approving multi-factor authentication (MFA). Plus, they note: O-UNC-053 operators change the themes of their phishing domains about every four to six weeks, and they also post claimed victims on ShinyHunters’ data leak site. In November, however, organizations targeted by O-UNC-053 began appearing on a new data leak site branded as Inception and not ShinyHunters. The first five - Advanced Micro Devices, Cigna Healthcare, Paychex, PepsiCo, and Henry Schein - appeared November 17 on the site, and all were marked “leaked.” Soon after, security maven Dominic Alvieri questioned if Inception was linked to ShinyHunters. “ShinyHunters are not all in jail,” he wrote on social media. On November 19, AutoZone appeared on the site, with Inception again claiming to have leaked the auto-parts retailer's files. On Saturday, EV technology firm Lucid Group joined the claimed victims. technology.title: Amazon scoops up AI accelerator tech to keep chips busy at all times
technology.description: Amazon has agreed to buy AI optimization technology from an Israeli startup in a bid to speed up its inference operations. The house of Bezos on Monday announced a deal to purchase proprietary AI acceleration tech from Decart AI, known as the Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), for an undisclosed amount. Amazon also plans to bring Decart’s three founders and their engineering team into the fold. Decart’s DOS is designed to push AI hardware closer to its maximum performance across different AI models and hardware platforms. The company claims that most AI chips live their lives without reaching their full potential – practically a sin in this age of increased hardware costs and limited availability – and DOS aims to fix that by operating between the model and the chip, optimizing kernels, compilers, and runtimes for the underlying hardware “so every core stays busy.” DOS is hardware-agnostic, with Decart saying it supports Nvidia GPUs, Google TPUs, and, most critically for our purposes here, AWS Trainium chips. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost,” Peter DeSantis, Amazon SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, and quantum computing, said in the announcement. “That's the pillar Trainium and our AI efforts are built on, and from our earliest work with Decart, we knew they … would help us push it even further.” Decart doesn’t offer much in the way of details about its proprietary AI-maxxing tech, but claims it can reduce latency, improve throughput, and reduce the costs associated with training and inference runs. An Amazon spokesperson clarified to The Register that the deal is an asset purchase and not a full company acquisition, with Amazon only acquiring DOS and the tech behind it as well as personnel. As for what may become of Decart after the deal, that’s unclear. Amazon told us to reach out to Decart to learn what may happen to any remaining employees and the company’s other technology, but we didn’t hear back. Along with offering its optimization stack, Decart has a couple of different AI models: Lucy, a live video model marketed toward advertisers, live streamers, and the like; and Oasis, a world model AI marketed toward companies working on embodied AI applications. Decart’s non-DOS assets weren’t mentioned in the press release, and per the Amazon spokesperson we talked to, that means they weren’t part of the deal. We can’t imagine that the Decart team is too upset about the potential abandonment of those models, though: While neither company has disclosed a price, Bloomberg claims its sources value the deal at around $7.5 billion. If Bloomberg's figure is accurate, that would make this deal one of the most expensive in Amazon’s history, right between its $3.9 billion acquisition of One Medical and its $8.5 billion purchase of film studio MGM . ®

science.title: Will astronauts farm on the moon? Scientists successfully grow potatoes in simulated lunar dust
science.description:
Julian Dossett is a freelance writer living in Santa Fe, New Mexico. He primarily covers the rocket industry and space exploration and, in addition to science writing, contributes travel stories to New Mexico Magazine. In 2022 and 2024, his travel writing earned IRMA Awards. Previously, he worked as a staff writer at CNET. He graduated from Texas State University in San Marcos in 2011 with a B.A. in philosophy. He owns a large collection of sci-fi pulp magazines from the 1960s.

It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon. The space agency even plans to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home. But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon. To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. The researchers published their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal. "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, said in a statement . "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon." To grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to regolith , the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. The moon contains various regions with unique surface makeups, so the materials they used simulated regolith from both lunar mare and lunar highland regions. The secret ingredient was vermicompost, a soil that's rich in nutrients. The team added different levels of vermicompost to the simulated regolith to grow the potatoes. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil. Oregon State University researchers David Handy and Aymeric Goyer studying potatoes grown in lunar regolith. (Image credit: Aymeric Goyer/David Handy/OSU) "We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, said in the same statement. The idea is that astronauts in the future could bring a little nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with regolith to grow potatoes. After all, it'd cost a ton to ship all that food from Earth. NASA funding supported this research.

Sports in space have a long and proud tradition, whether it's Alan Shepard playing golf on the moon or the crew of the ISS hosting their own version of the Summer Olympics . The future looks bright as well, with the foundation of the Space Games Federation , the self-described "first governing and sanctioning body for competitive sports played in zero or micro-gravity," co-founded by a NASA astronaut. Not to be outdone, science fiction has expanded the idea of zero-g and low-gravity sports to their logical extent, imagining everything from Doctor Who's zero-g squash to the advanced, gamified combat simulations of Ender's Game. There was even Space Jam 's alien basketball game for the fate of the planet, though the gravity-defying antics there come from cartoon shenanigans rather than a zero-g playing field. As humanity edges closer to colonizing our neighbors through projects like the Artemis Program and its ambition to establish habitats on the moon, our imaginations have to expand to encompass not only how we'll live in space but also how we'll play. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 23, 2015: Blue Origin sticks 1st-ever rocket landing from space with its suborbital New Shepard rocket
science.description: null On Nov. 23, 2015, a Blue Origin rocket made a historic landing. Before this time, all rockets were single-use only — even SpaceX's rockets. Blue Origin changed the concept forever. After launching the New Shepard capsule safely into space, the rocket started heading back to Earth. It flew towards a landing pad, reignited its engine to slow down and touched down softly on the ground . This was the first successful vertical landing from space in history. The Blue Origin milestone meant that rockets could be reused for multiple missions, which saves money and reduces waste. (Image credit: Blue Origin) Why it mattered Today, SpaceX may be the most well-known for landing its Falcon 9 rocket boosters from orbit. The company's triple-core Falcon Heavy boosters can also land vertically and its massive Starship megarocket can even return to the launch site to be caught by giant metal arms. But in the end, Blue Origin did it first. Blue Origin's New Shepard booster landing kicked off an era of vertical launch and vertical landings for rockets that continues to this day. It may have even outlasted the New Shepard rocket. Since that first landing, Blue Origin has launched 17 suborbital astronaut flights with New Shepard, and 21 more uncrewed flights for a total of 38 missions between April 2015 and 2026. The company reused its New Shepard boosters repeatedly (though it did lose one during an uncrewed launch after a technical issue.) But in January 2026, the company announced a pause in New Shepard flights for two years so that it could focus on moon lander projects. But Blue Origin did not abandon rocket landings. Indeed, the company's success with New Shepard led it to build vertical landing into its larger orbital rocket, New Glenn, which made its first successful landing 2025 — nearly 10 years after that first touchdown. Blue Origin has since reflown a New Glenn booster , and is developing a new rocket engine called Northstar for even better performance. Want more space history? While their appearances may be unusual, these formations offer scientists something far more valuable than a collection of curious snapshots: clues to the geological processes that shaped Mars over billions of years. In particular, the rocks and mineral deposits could help researchers piece together the planet's watery past and identify environments that may once have been capable of supporting microbial life. NASA's Curiosity rover recently wrapped up a drilling campaign at a location nicknamed "Nazca," where scientists have been examining unusual disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in the surrounding bedrock. Some of the features are so thin and flat that the mission team likened them to potato chips, according to a statement from the space agency. NASA's Curiosity rover captured a close-up view of unusual, disk-shaped crystal formations embedded in Martian bedrock using its Mars Hand Lens Imager (MAHLI) on Nov. 7, 2026 (Sol 5067). science.title: The remains of a long-dead volcano on Mars | Space photo of the day for Nov. 23, 2026
science.description: null An image of Tharsis Tholus, a volcano on the surface of Mars, produced by ESA's Mars Express orbiter. (Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) Researchers have spotted an ancient, "dead" Martian volcano from orbit around the Red Planet. What is it? The European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft, which has been orbiting and studying the planet since it arrived in 2003, recently captured incredible new imagery of the volcano Tharsis Tholus. This snapshot was captured by the spacecraft's High Resolution Stereo Camera. Even as old and worn as it is, the Martian volcano stands at around 4.97 miles (8 kilometers) tall which is comparable to some of the highest peaks in the Himalayan mountains. Despite its impressive height, it's still only about a medium-sized volcano for Mars, which is home much more impressively-sized volcanoes. For example, the planet's largest volcano Olympus Mons measures in at roughly 13.2 miles high (21.3 kilometers). Tharsis Tholus, a volcano on the surface of Mars, as seen by ESA's Mars Express orbiter. (Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) Why is it incredible? While Tharsis Tholus might not be the tallest volcano on Mars, it is incredibly steep. It is steeper than Mauna Kea in Hawaii on Earth. To fully showcase the volcano's structure and topography in 3D, researchers actually exaggerated the vertical scale in this image, ESA reported . In addition to being steep and fairly tall, the volcano also has an interesting history. You can see that it is speckled with what look like small holes which are actually craters created by impacts from objects like asteroids. The volcano's current, unique shape is a combined effort by these impacts, environmental factors causing erosion and warping and ancient lava flows that left behind built-up material. The observations by Mars Express also reveals cracks and other imperfections in the volcano. All of these details might seem like superficial bits of detail, however every small crater, every lumpy cliffside and every worn down surface hides information about the planet's past. By studying features like volcanoes on Mars, researchers can piece together what the planet may have looked like in its ancient past. How active was this volcano? How did it interact with the landscape around it? Observations like this can hold the answers.

science.title: COP31 collapse has shattered the pretence of a global climate consensus
science.description: A closing plenary session at the COP31 climate summit on 22 November AP Photo/Khalil Hamra/Alamy A deep rift among nations on how to tackle climate change, and whether the global economy can be weaned off fossil fuels, was exposed after the spectacular collapse of talks at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. After a tortuous fortnight of negotiations, COP31 ended in disarray late on 22 November after countries including the UK and the EU refused to agree to a political accord that failed to mention fossil fuels. Read more Can everyone live a ‘good life’ without destroying the planet? The Antalya pact would have seen countries officially recognise that the world is on course to exceed 1.5°C degrees of warming and promise to limit the scale of the overshoot as far as possible. It also would have committed nations to increasing the share of electricity in total final energy consumption to 35 per cent globally by 2035, a key target for climate campaigners who see electrification as the route away from fossil-fuel dependency. Advertisement But the draft agreement proved unacceptable to many countries, including the UK, the EU and some small island nations, after all mentions of fossil fuels were omitted at the behest of fossil fuel-dependent nations such as Saudi Arabia and Russia. Failing to mention fossil fuels explicitly in the text would have marked a backwards step for the climate process, the EU argued. At COP28 in Dubai three years ago, nations agreed to “transition away from fossil fuels” , but since then, attempts to strengthen the language or clarify how this transition will take place have been blocked by petrostates. Alden Meyer at the climate think tank E3G says the talks were subjected to a “brutish” strategy from fossil fuel-exporting states to “systematically block” any reference to the COP28 deal. “They clearly have buyer’s remorse about that agreement. They never were happy about it.” Free newsletter Sign up to The Earth Edition Sign up to newsletter The EU also took issue with a paragraph inserted at the behest of Saudi Arabia – which leads the 22-member Arab group of countries – calling for the rapid growth of carbon capture and storage technologies to the gigatonne scale by 2035. Carbon capture and storage technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and many sceptics are concerned that focusing on them will justify the continued use of fossil fuels and distract from the deep emissions cuts necessary for controlling climate change. Ireland’s climate minister Darragh O’ Brien, speaking on behalf of the EU, claimed the negotiations had been “hijacked by fossil fuel producers” and said the EU would “not accept a COP that greenwashes fossil fuels”. science.title: What did the Soviet Union's final deep space probe actually see on Mars?
science.description:
Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

On July 12, 1988, Phobos 2 — one of the Soviet Union's final major planetary exploration probes — was launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome aboard a Proton rocket. The spacecraft's mission included the study of Mars and the Martian moon Phobos, with a planned close approach and deployment of landing probes, and over the next several months, the spacecraft successfully captured more than three dozen images of Phobos during its time in service. However, early in the following year, the spacecraft's mission abruptly ended after the Phobos 2 ground team mysteriously lost contact with the spacecraft. Adding to the mystery were objects in some of the final photographs dispatched by the doomed spacecraft, which seemed to show an elongated shadow beneath the probe — a strange twist in one of the Soviet Union's final space missions, and one that soon gave rise to conspiracy theories about what the fate of Phobos 2 might have been. So what caused the odd-looking appearance of the shadow in the final images captured by Phobos 2, and what was the real reason behind the spacecraft's sudden failure? Last of the Soviet space explorers Originally, the Soviet Union had planned for Phobos 2 to reach the Red Planet by late January 1989, after which the spacecraft would begin collecting data about the Martian environment leading up to its initial contact with Mars' largest moon in early June. A model of one of the Phobos spacecraft on display in the Memorial Museum of Cosmonautics in Moscow, Russia. (Image credit: Музей Космонавтики from Россия, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons) To say that a lot hinged on the success of the mission would be an understatement, given the unfortunate fate of the probe's predecessor, Phobos 1, which went offline on Sept. 2, 1988, after a faulty command sequence was initiated while the spacecraft was on its way to Mars. The stakes were almost immediately raised as Phobos 2 arrived in orbit around Mars on Jan. 30, 1989 , when one of the probe's three onboard flight system processors was found to have gone offline, with another already experiencing technical issues. Over the course of the next several weeks, Phobos 2 was able to overcome some of these setbacks and successfully began sending useful scientific data about the Martian environment back to Earth. By March, all the probe's science instruments appeared to be functioning normally, and despite the earlier loss of one of its processors, the remaining two had continued to facilitate control of the spacecraft by its Soviet ground control team. science.title: Astronomers just discovered a rare triple star system 28 light-years away, and they have ‘no clean explanation for how it got here’
science.description: A triple system containing a dim red dwarf star and not one but two white dwarfs has been fortuitously discovered just 28 light-years away from our solar system. "We were actually looking for planets ," Étienne Artigau of the Trottier Institute for Research on Exoplanets at the Université de Montréal, who led the discovery, said in a statement . "Instead, we found something much more surprising." So surprising that there are no similar systems within at least 100 light-years . Furthermore, the configuration of the system seems impossible. "This system should not exist," added Montreal's Patrick Dufour. "We have no clean explanation for how it got here." This triple system has been called Welopō'ai, which is a portmanteau of two Hawaiian words that means a 'path of family traits', and to understand the mystery behind it requires astronomers to figure out the history of the three objects. A white dwarf is what remains when a star of similar mass to our sun reaches the end of its life. As it begins to run low on hydrogen for nuclear fusion reactions in its core, the star's energy generation begins to falter and its interior starts to contract under gravity . This has the effect of raising the temperature throughout the star, causing an outer shell of hydrogen to ignite its own fusion reactions. The star promptly bloats to become a red giant tens or even hundreds of millions of kilometers across. Soon enough the star ceases fusion reactions completely. The star's outer layers are shed and they expand out into space, while its core contracts to become an inert white dwarf with a diameter similar to Earth but with a mass generally between half and two-thirds of a solar mass . Therefore, the Welopō'ai system was once a triple system with two sun-like stars plus the red dwarf. Now the two sun-like stars have undergone this stage of star death while their companion red dwarf continues to linger, since its low mass bequeaths it a longer life because it does not use up its core hydrogen as quickly. One of the white dwarfs orbits the red dwarf at a distance of 129.3 astronomical units (19.3 billion kilometers or 12 billion miles) and takes about 1,000 years to complete one orbit. This white dwarf and the red dwarf were previously known, and Artigau's team had been using the SPectropolarimètre InfraROUge (SPIRou) instrument on the Canada–France–Hawaii Telescope atop Mauna Kea to search for planets orbiting the red dwarf when they noticed something highly unusual. NASA Earth Observatory/Lauren Dauphin More than 60 years ago, scientists at NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center aimed a laser skyward and fired a pulse of light at an orbiting satellite equipped with special reflectors. By measuring the time it took for the light to return, they demonstrated a new, more precise method for tracking satellites. Since then, satellite laser ranging (SLR) has grown more precise and more widely used. The technique now underpins many aspects of Earth observation, such as validating satellite orbits and mapping subtle changes to Earth’s surface. Pioneered at the Goddard Optical Research Facility—now the Goddard Geophysical and Astronomical Observatory —laser ranging is performed at more than 40 stations worldwide. In 2026, the next generation of SLR, developed by NASA scientists and tested at Goddard, began to come online. On October 12, a faster, even more precise SLR system officially debuted at the Ny-Ålesund Geodetic Observatory in Svalbard, Norway, operated by the Norwegian Mapping Authority, a NASA partner. It is the first NASA next-generation SLR system in operation and the northernmost SLR facility on Earth. While the systems developed decades ago have been “workhorses” of the global laser tracking network, their age and the growing number of satellites have necessitated updates, said Stephen Merkowitz, project manager for NASA’s Space Geodesy Project . “We wanted newer systems that could track more objects, and track them more accurately and precisely,” he said. science.description: null Amazon's first satellite launch since a rocket failure doomed 40 of its spacecraft is set for Tuesday morning (Nov. 24), and you can watch the action live. An Ariane 6 rocket carrying 36 satellites for the Amazon Leo constellation is scheduled to lift off from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou, French Guiana, on Tuesday (Nov. 23), during a 29-minute window that opens at 5:45 a.m. EST (1045 GMT; 7:45 a.m. local time in Kourou). You can watch it live here at Space.com courtesy of Arianespace, the French company that operates the Ariane 6. Coverage will begin at 5:15 a.m. EST (1015 GMT). The launch was originally supposed to take place on Monday (Nov. 23), but that attempt was scrubbed due to a technical issue affecting the rocket's ground support systems, according to Arianespace . Amazon Leo, so named because it will operate in low Earth orbit , will compete with SpaceX's Starlink internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 operational spacecraft. Amazon's network will eventually have more than 3,200 satellites, but just 400 or so have reached orbit to date. Another 40 were supposed to be delivered on Nov. 15, but they were lost after their rocket ride, a United Launch Alliance (ULA) Vulcan Centaur , suffered a problem shortly after launch. Ariane 6 and Vulcan Centaur aren't the only rockets Amazon is depending on to build its broadband constellation. Jeff Bezos' company has also booked rides on ULA's Atlas V rocket, Blue Origin's New Glenn and SpaceX's Falcon 9 . Vulcan will be grounded for a while as ULA investigates the Nov. 15 failure and works to fix whatever caused it. And New Glenn hasn't flown since April, when the rocket failed to deliver AST SpaceMobile's BlueBird 7 satellite to the proper orbit. New Glenn's return to flight was further complicated on May 28, when the rocket exploded during a routine prelaunch test. The Ariane 6, the successor to Arianespace's Ariane 5 heavy lifter, debuted in July 2024 and has nine launches under its belt to date. All of them have been successful except that maiden mission, which was a partial failure. The upcoming mission will be the fourth Amazon Leo flight for the Ariane 6, following launches in February, April and June of this year. NASA/Robert Markowitz For 65 years, NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston has helped shape human spaceflight, from the Gemini missions that demonstrated rendezvous and docking techniques needed for Apollo to the research conducted aboard the International Space Station, which has supported a continuous human presence for more than 26 years. Today, Johnson teams are preparing crews and systems for NASA’s next chapter: returning astronauts to the lunar surface and building the capabilities needed for a long-term human presence at the Moon. Across those missions, generations of flight controllers, engineers, scientists, instructors, medical specialists, and other experts have helped crews live and work beyond Earth. Johnson is home to NASA’s Orion and Moon Base programs, and its teams continue to support space station operations, astronaut training, spacecraft development, mission operations, and human health. Mercury and Gemini: Preparing for Apollo When the Manned Spacecraft Center officially opened on Nov. 1, 1961, NASA had already flown two suborbital Mercury missions, with the first orbital flight just months away. Most Project Mercury activities remained at Cape Canaveral in Florida to maintain continuity, but the new Project Gemini took up residence in Houston, housed in temporary leased facilities across the city while construction of the new Clear Lake campus continued. The new Mission Control Center became NASA’s primary flight control center in June 1965, with the Gemini IV mission that included the first American spacewalk. Houston became the nerve center for American human spaceflight, overseeing the remaining eight Gemini missions before transitioning to the Apollo program. Following the tragic Apollo 1 fire in January 1967, managers, engineers, and astronauts at the Manned Spacecraft Center applied lessons learned to make the spacecraft safer and ensure the safety of its astronauts, resuming crewed missions in October 1968. Managers in Houston devised a daring plan to send Apollo 8 on a circumlunar flight. In December 1968, Apollo 8 made its historic trip around the Moon, and seven months later Apollo 11 astronauts Neil Armstrong and Edwin “Buzz” Aldrin landed on the lunar surface. Their first voice transmission back to Earth after their arrival began with the word “Houston.” Five more Moon landings completed the Apollo program and humanity’s first phase of lunar exploration in December 1972. Following the Moon landings, scientists at the Manned Spacecraft Center’s Lunar Receiving Laboratory conducted initial analyses of Apollo lunar samples and prepared them for researchers around the world. science.title: This viral star projector has been hyped to Mars and back, but we hunted down the best version you can buy
science.description: It was only a matter of time, but AI has come for astronomy accessories. I’ve yet to see a fictional elderly craftsman begging you to buy his hand-carved telescopes; however, it has absolutely muddied the waters around this viral gooseneck Galaxy Projector Night Light. The good news is that there is an impressive little star projector to be had here, and I’m here to cut through the AI-assisted hype. To make sure you’re not hoodwinked, I’ve done the online legwork to bring you the best version of this device, and it won’t cost you a fortune to put a planetarium in your pocket. Before we dive into what makes this Galaxy Projector Night Light so great, there are a couple of pressing issues to address. No variant of this USB-powered star projector will break up heated dinner arguments by casting a beautifully animated space whale on the ceiling, as one ridiculous AI-generated advert asserts. Its projections are eye-catching enough to entertain space fans young and old, but they’re strictly static. Also, while you might be tempted by the lure of 24 interchangeable slides, compared to this Galaxy Projector Night Light’s 13, this lesser model’s slide selection is a letdown. Not only are the slides smaller and blurrier than this model, a large number are dedicated to seasonal holidays. As much as I enjoy Christmas, if I had Santa’s colossal face gazing down at me from the ceiling I’d never sleep again. Zanbix 2 in 1 Galaxy Projector Night Light review More than meets the eye Aside from the projector itself, the Zanbix 2 in 1 Galaxy Projector Night Light includes 13 swappable slides, crammed into a compact box. (Image credit: Chris McMullen) I tempered my expectations when I first got my hands on the Galaxy Projector Night Light. Packed in a small, relatively unassuming box, it looks remarkably similar to the standard model that’s spread across TikTok, YouTube, Facebook and so on. Just like that one, it’s powered via USB, with a flexible stalk, a slot for slides and a nose-mounted focus wheel. However, once I hooked it up to a handy USB socket, all my reservations vanished, and I was seriously impressed by the power of this little projector. You’ll need a darkened room but the Galaxy Projector Night Light’s larger lens is a serious step-up from the run-of-the-mill version. Its images are richer and clearer than you’d expect from a projector this size, and easily capable of transforming a mid-sized ceiling or wall into a cosmic display. This stunning image of the Pillars of Creation originally came from the James Webb Space Telescope. (Image credit: Chris McMullen) This stunning James Webb Space Telescope image of the Pillars of Creation, with its vast columns of gas and dust, is a perfect example of the projections on offer. The fact the display was static didn’t diminish its wow factor, and I spent a good 15 minutes gazing at it in wonder.
